articles.title: Erlang Actors vs Java Virtual Threads: What Staroletov (2026) Teaches Us About Concurrency Design
articles.excerpt: Erlang Actors vs Java Virtual Threads: What Staroletov (2026) Teaches Us About Concurrency Design Java finally has lightweight threads. Erlang has had them since 1986. But the gap between the two is n…
articles.body: Erlang Actors vs Java Virtual Threads: What Staroletov (2026) Teaches Us About Concurrency Design Java finally has lightweight threads. Erlang has had them since 1986. But the gap between the two is not about raw concurrency numbers — it is about what happens when things go wrong. In his 2026 Erlang Workshop paper “Modern Erlang Teaching from Code Refactoring to Actor System Verification,” Sergey Staroletov draws a direct contrast between Erlang’s actor model and Java’s modern virtual threads (Project Loom). His point is not that one is faster. It is that both enable high concurrency, but only one bakes fault isolation and hierarchical supervision into the language design from the ground up.

articles.title: I built a 3D survival game in a weekend and shipped it from my own PC
articles.excerpt: I wanted to see how far a weekend build could go, so I made a 3D survival game — dodge incoming fire, and don’t get sandwiched by enemies. The whole thing runs on a bare Node HTTP server on my local m…
articles.body: I wanted to see how far a weekend build could go, so I made a 3D survival game — dodge incoming fire, and don’t get sandwiched by enemies. The whole thing runs on a bare Node HTTP server on my local machine and is exposed via a tunnel. No frameworks, no build steps, just plain ES modules. The most fun part was balancing the difficulty. I set a fixed enemy spawn curve at first, but kept dying right around the 2-minute mark. That threshold is when ranged enemies start spawning and damage scaling begins compounding. Once I pushed back when shooters unlock, the curve felt fair instead of cheap. My personal best is 4:39. A solid run should last roughly 10–14 minutes. How long can you survive?

articles.body: If you are asking about the Cosmos ATOM unbonding period and what happens after 21 days, the short answer is that the chain moves your tokens back to your available balance automatically. On the Cosmos Hub, there is normally no separate claim or withdraw step. If the time has passed and your balance looks wrong, there is usually a checkable reason. This guide shows how to find your exact completion time, confirm what happened on-chain, and work through the common causes. Cosmos ATOM unbonding period: what happens after 21 days When you undelegate ATOM, the tokens enter an unbonding state. They stop earning staking rewards, and you cannot transfer them yet. The Cosmos Hub's unbonding period has long been set at 21 days, but it is a chain parameter that governance can change.

articles.title: I love big Si-C batteries, but slow charging is a steep price to pay
articles.excerpt: Bigger batteries sound great, but are slower charging speeds worth the extra capacity?
articles.body: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority If there’s been one major game changer for smartphone hardware in the past few years, it’s undoubtedly the adoption of silicon-carbon (Si-C) battery technology. By mixing traditional lithium-ion cells with silicon-carbon, manufacturers are able to greatly increase a battery’s storage capacity without a huge increase in its physical size, meaning better longevity for our smartphones. Even small amounts of added Si-C have been a game changer for battery capacities. After being stuck with 5,000mAh Li-ion cells as the upper limit for the best part of a decade, we’ve quickly seen capacities jump to 7,000mAh, 8,000mAh, and even 10,000mAh cells in the most advanced cases.
